---
title: "End to end: a simulated ensemble against the published one"
author: "Simon Frost"
engine: julia
---

## Overview

This vignette closes the loop. It compares an ensemble of communities simulated with this
package (`scripts/simulate_dataset.jl`) with the authors' Dataset S1/S2, first metric by
metric and then through the paper's analysis: correlations by size class, modular groups, and
how correlations change with community size.

```{julia}
using DominguezGarcia2019
using CSV, DataFrames, Statistics, Random, Printf
using Plots
data = joinpath(pkgdir(DominguezGarcia2019), "data")
sim_raw = CSV.read(joinpath(data, "simulated", "ensemble_v4.csv"), DataFrame)
pub_raw = CSV.read(joinpath(data, "dominguez-garcia2019", "Dataset_S2.csv"), DataFrame)
(simulated = nrow(sim_raw), published = nrow(pub_raw),
 median_seconds_per_community = median(sim_raw.seconds))
```

Each simulated community was drawn with initial richness uniform on 5–110 and its own random
seed (`Sim<seed>`), so every row can be regenerated.

The raw columns follow the published convention (`community_record`, `convention = :published`).
`Amax` and `tmax` come from the ∞-norm of the propagator, and the four median metrics use the
published pulse weights, which are misaligned after extinctions (`published_pulse_covariance`).
The SI's versions of these six columns are kept as `*_si` (see
`lab/wiki/analysis/published-conventions.md`).

## The metrics, size by size

```{julia}
bins = 5:10:105
binned(df, col) = [let v = df[(df.N .>= b) .& (df.N .< b + 10), col]
                       isempty(v) ? NaN : median(v)        # the published data stop at N = 99
                   end for b in bins]
cols = [:Rinf, :R0, :Amax, :tmax, :MR0, :Is, :TM_p, :minTM_i, :av_TM_i, :Ext_half, :RM_p, :Robst, :Btot, :Nb]
plot([plot(bins .+ 5, binned(pub_raw, c); label = "published", lw = 2, title = string(c), titlefontsize = 9,
           legend = c === :Rinf ? :topright : false) for c in cols]...; layout = (4, 4), size = (950, 800))
for (k, c) in enumerate(cols)
    plot!(bins .+ 5, binned(sim_raw, c); subplot = k, label = "simulated", lw = 2)
end
current()
```

Medians by richness, in the raw columns of the dataset (before the sign changes of the
analysis). The calibration targets were total biomass and the number of plants. The other
panels are independent checks of the reconstructed simulator.

## The analysis on simulated communities

The published Dataset S2 has 100 communities at each richness. The 10,000 simulated
communities give about as many per richness (the median is printed below), so correlations at
a single richness are about as noisy in both; class averages pool 11 sizes.

```{julia}
sim = prepare_metrics(sim_raw)
pub = read_metrics(joinpath(data, "dominguez-garcia2019", "Dataset_S2.csv"))
analysed = 5 .<= sim.N .<= 99
share_varying(v) = 1 - maximum(count(==(x), v) for x in unique(v)) / length(v)
variation = DataFrame(metric = METRICS,
                      simulated = [share_varying(sim[analysed, l]) for l in METRICS],
                      published = [share_varying(pub[!, l]) for l in METRICS])
filter(r -> min(r.simulated, r.published) < 0.5, variation)
```

Only the median maximal amplification and its time take few distinct values: a median pulse
either grows (MAmax > 1) or the metrics are exactly `(1, 0)`. The published communities
amplify in 22% of cases; ours do in
`{julia} count(sim_raw.MAmax[analysed] .> 1 + 1e-12)` of `{julia} count(analysed)`. With the
SI's aligned weights (`MAmax_si`) almost none do
(`{julia} count(sim_raw.MAmax_si[analysed] .> 1 + 1e-12)`), so the two metrics would be
constant. The comparison below uses every metric that varies in at least 1% of communities in
both datasets.

```{julia}
labels = filter(r -> min(r.simulated, r.published) >= 0.01, variation).metric
sc_sim = size_correlations(sim; labels, rng = Xoshiro(2019))   # up to 100 communities per richness
sc_pub = size_correlations(pub; labels, rng = Xoshiro(2019))
(metrics = length(labels), sizes = length(sc_sim.sizes), median_per_size = median(sc_sim.n))
```

```{julia}
upper(R) = [R[i, j] for j in axes(R, 2) for i in axes(R, 1) if i < j]
plots = map(SIZE_CLASSES) do (name, (lo, hi))
    Rs, _ = class_average(sc_sim, lo, hi)
    Rp, _ = class_average(sc_pub, lo, hi)
    x, y = upper(Rp), upper(Rs)
    scatter(x, y; ms = 2, alpha = 0.6, label = false, xlabel = "published ρ", ylabel = "simulated ρ",
            title = @sprintf("%s: r = %.2f", name, cor(x, y)), xlim = (-1, 1), ylim = (-1, 1), aspect_ratio = 1)
    plot!([-1, 1], [-1, 1]; label = false, color = :grey)
end
plot(plots...; layout = (1, 3), size = (950, 340))
```

Each point is one of the 300 pairs of metrics: its mean correlation in a size class in the
published data against the simulated data. Points on the diagonal mean the simulator
reproduces that relationship.

```{julia}
function groups_table(sc, lo, hi)
    R, _ = class_average(sc, lo, hi)
    g, Q = modular_groups(metric_network(R); runs = 50, rng = Xoshiro(1))
    return g, Q
end
rand_index(a, b) = mean((a[i] == a[j]) == (b[i] == b[j]) for i in eachindex(a) for j in eachindex(a) if i < j)
for (name, (lo, hi)) in SIZE_CLASSES
    gs, Qs = groups_table(sc_sim, lo, hi)
    gp, Qp = groups_table(sc_pub, lo, hi)
    @printf("%-6s Q simulated %.3f, published %.3f; Rand index of the partitions %.2f\n", name, Qs, Qp,
            rand_index(gs, gp))
    foreach(k -> println("   ", join(sc_sim.labels[gs .== k], " ")), 1:maximum(gs))
end
```

The Rand index is the share of pairs of metrics on which the two partitions agree (together in
both, or apart in both).

## How correlations change with size

```{julia}
t_sim = combine(groupby(correlation_types(sc_sim), :type), nrow => :simulated)
t_pub = combine(groupby(correlation_types(sc_pub), :type), nrow => :published)
sort(outerjoin(t_pub, t_sim; on = :type), :type)
```

The classes are those of SI §1, Fig. S1: G unchanged; E and F strengthen or weaken from small
to medium communities, then stay constant; B and C keep strengthening or weakening; A and D
change sign.
